3. The intended loaded rollback

A complete failed second-end recovery would have to perform the following physical sequence.

Preserve the preceding supported state.
Retain the previous frame through the stationary holder and support the workpiece’s gravity through the independent floor cradle.

Enclose the failure before escalating proof.
The cage surrounds the prospective contact and counterhold. Signal contacts, keys, shafts and temporary tool contacts must either lie inside it or have separately observed withdrawal.

Identify the outer load that remains.
Observe the separate support and contact reactions. A small common resultant is insufficient evidence.

Meter the outer reaction through a continuously retained path.
The screw remains engaged while the outer force is reduced. The model does not remove a contact and then assume that the structure settles safely.

Open the exceptional interface.
Withdraw the cup halves, observe real clearance and retract every crossing drive element.

Release the first end and transfer the complete member.
The first end uses the ordinary interface. Gravity support passes through the floor cradle, main machine and rack receiver with individually observed load return.

Dissipate internal energy at the rack.
The cage remains retained while the contact and counterlinks are unloaded through finite drives and brakes.

Quarantine and restore.
The failed assembly remains identified and unavailable. A replacement cassette and compatible member come from finite stock; later refurbishment is paid.

Steps 5–7 still contain missing physical transitions. In particular, the rack model assumes a retained dock that has not yet been completed for positive normal retention, all constrained reactions and the full withdrawal route. The main machine cannot be declared free to leave merely because a scalar rack calculation reaches its terminal condition.
